problem: Topological-map VLN methods (DUET, BEVBert) re-run GCN-like/dual-scale models over the whole graph at every step, which is costly. Their node-based (undirected) panorama features are also coarse and direction-invariant, so they need extra fine-grained branches (local views, BEV) that add more cost.
motivation: Global action planning over the explored map helps VLN, but recomputing the entire map each step is wasteful when only a few nodes change. Navigation is inherently directional, and the same node passed from different directions should have different representations; instruction-path alignment is what the agent really needs to judge.
key_idea: Plan by scoring the alignment between the instruction and the directed fidelity trajectory (detour-free path from start) to each unvisited node, with paths represented as sequences of orientation-aware directed edge features and computed incrementally only for new nodes.
insight: Directed edge features beat undirected node panorama features (SPL 65.16 vs 56.77 on R2R val unseen), showing directionality removes redundant panorama information. The module ablation shows OPE contributes the most (removing it drops SPL from 65.16 to 57.32) and CCM adds about 2 SPL (63.07 without it). Causal mask plus KV-cache sharing over common path prefixes yields large compute savings (0.9 GFLOPs vs 35.5 for BEVBert at 10 steps) with comparable accuracy.
method: Directed graph with edge features: the explored area is a directed graph where each edge stores the visual observation when facing that direction from a node, giving consistent representations for visited and unvisited nodes.

Orientation-aware Panorama Encoder (OPE): 2-layer transformer decoder where relative heading/elevation of an edge is the query attending to panorama view tokens (view features + orientation), yielding edge features.
Fidelity trajectory stack: for each unvisited node, a stack-maintained path from the start with detours removed by popping on backtrack.

Matching Assessment Module (MAM): 4-layer transformer decoder cross-attending path edge tokens (with position embeddings, learnable start/stop tokens) to text; last token is the path embedding stored on the node. Multiple new paths are computed in one pass via a merged causal mask and KV-cache of the shared prefix.

Candidate Comparison Module (CCM): a single transformer layer over all unvisited-node path embeddings plus an MLP gives scores; softmax picks the temporary target (or the stop node), and the agent moves there along the shortest path.

Training: MLM pretraining on PREVALENT augmented data (Marky for RxR), then fine-tuning with a mix of teacher forcing and student forcing with pseudo labels (lambda=0.2). Text encoder is ALBEF 6-layer (mRoBERTa for RxR), and features come from DINOv2 or CLIP.

setting.backbone: ALBEF 6-layer text encoder (mRoBERTa 12-layer for RxR) + OPE/MAM/CCM transformers, trained; DINOv2 or CLIP-ViT-B image features
setting.training_data: R2R/RxR training sets plus PREVALENT augmented data for R2R (pretraining and fine-tuning) and Marky augmented data for RxR; MLM pretraining
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (pre-extracted view features) with neighbor node orientations and coordinates; no depth
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints (global selection of unvisited nodes plus stop)

numbers_note: Table 3 also reports Ours (CLIP features) on R2R val unseen at one decimal (TL 12.2, NE 3.1, SR 71.0, SPL 62.7) with efficiency figures; the ablations use the DINOv2 model (SR 73.78, SPL 65.16).
results: On R2R, PRET (DINOv2) reaches val-unseen SR 74 / SPL 65 and test-unseen SR 72 / SPL 64, comparable to BEVBert (val-unseen SR 75 / SPL 64, test-unseen SR 73 / SPL 62), at about 3% of its decoder GFLOPs at 10 steps. On RxR val unseen it beats BEVBert with sDTW 62.4 vs 58.6 and SR 72.8 vs 68.5.
limitations: Navigation sometimes requires environment layout information that the model lacks; val-seen performance is sub-optimal versus BEVBert and Meta-Explore.
Uses pre-extracted fixed visual features and is evaluated only in discrete simulated environments (R2R, RxR), not in continuous environments or on real robots.
Comparisons use augmented data, and the reported compute omits the text and visual encoders.
